claims.source: Upon stimulation with soluble chemokines, transiently (not shown) as well as stably transfected cells showed a time dependent phosphorylation of ERK 1/2 (Figure 6A), which was not the case in non-transfected cells (compare Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Stably transfected LOX cells expressing C-terminally truncated tm-chemokine variants lacking the intracellular domain cannot be activated by stimulation with s-chemokines.
claims.source: As the short intracellular domain of tm-chemokines could be involved in this signal transduction, we performed corresponding experiments with C-terminally truncated tm-chemokines that lacked the complete intracellular but not the transmembrane domain (Figure 6B). In fact, this truncation abolished the signal transduction effects observed with the full-length tm-chemokines.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B demonstrating absence of ERK phosphorylation in cells expressing truncated tm-chemokines.

claims.claim: Conditioned media from tm-chemokine-transfected cells contain considerable amounts of corresponding s-chemokines.
claims.source: In fact, 24 hr- or 48 hr-conditioned media of tm-chemokine-transfected cells, but not of vector-transfected cells, contained considerable amounts of corresponding s-chemokines as detected by Western blot or ELISA (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Conditioned media from tm-chemokine-transfected cells induce ERK 1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine-expressing cells.
claims.source: As expected, conditioned media from transfected, but not from control cells, induced ERK 1/2 phosphorylation; again non- or control-transfected LOX cells yielded no signal transduction (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 significantly reduces the amount of cleaved PARP induced by Camptothecin.
claims.source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Stimulation of tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduces the amount of cleaved PARP induced by Camptothecin.
claims.source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Mock-transfected LOX cells are not rescued from Camptothecin-induced cell death by soluble chemokines.
claims.source: As shown by immunocytochemistry and Western blot, stimulation of tm-CXCL16-transfected LOX cells with s-CXCL16 and tm-CX3CL1-transfected LOX cells with s-CX3CL1 significantly reduced the amount of the cleaved Poly (ADP-Ribose) Polymerase (PARP), whereas mock-transfected LOX cells were not rescued (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry and Western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: siRNA silencing reduces tm-chemokine transcript amounts to 24-59% of controls transfected with unspecific control siRNAs.
claims.source: By siRNA silencing, tm-chemokine transcript amounts were reduced up to 24-59% of controls transfected with unspecific control siRNAs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: s-chemokine-mediated ERK-phosphorylation is clearly reduced in tm-chemokine silenced cells.
claims.source: The s-chemokine-mediated ERK-phosphorylation could be observed in control siRNA-treated glioma cell lines and primary cultures but was clearly reduced in tm-chemokine silenced cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Specific antibodies against the chemokine domains of CXCL16 or CX3CL1 induce ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
claims.source: To find out, whether antibodies against the chemokine domains of CXCL16 or CX3CL1 can also induce signaling of the tm-chemokines, we stimulated stably transfected tm-CXCL16 or tm-CX3CL1 LOX cells with 0.1 µg/ml of the respective antibody (Figure 9A); IgG from the same species and mock-transfected cells served as controls. In fact, specific antibodies, but not controls induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Monovalent F(ab) fragments of antibodies against chemokine domains do not induce signal transduction in tm-chemokine expressing cells.
claims.source: However, monovalent F(ab) fragments of the same antibodies generated by papain digestion and purification did not produce any effects in transfected cells (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Di/oligomerization of tm-chemokines is necessary for signal transduction.
claims.source: These experiments show that antibodies like soluble ligands induce signal transduction through tm-chemokines, and this process seems to depend on di/oligomerization of the tm-chemokines.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that intact antibodies but not monovalent F(ab) fragments induce signaling, as shown in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Dimerization of the chemokine domain of CX3CL1 has been shown by X-ray crystal structure.
claims.source: Similarly, di- and multimerization of the chemokine domain of CX3CL1 had already earlier been shown by X-ray crystal structure (Hoover et al., 2000), and is also known for some other (soluble) chemokines.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hoover et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Clustering/bundle formation of transmembrane CX3CL1 has been observed in transfected and primary cells by bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) and homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF).
claims.source: And indeed, a clustering/bundle formation of transmembrane CX3CL1 has been observed in transfected and primary cells by bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) and homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF; Hermand et al., 2008; Ostuni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hermand et al., 2008 and Ostuni et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The intracellular tails of transmembrane ligands contain signaling domains that are critical for signal transduction in reverse signaling.
claims.source: Signaling domains of the intracellular tails of transmembrane ligands seem to be critical for the signal transduction in reverse signaling, and thus also may transduce inverse signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about reverse signaling mechanisms and is supported by the experimental data showing the requirement of intracellular domains for inverse signaling.

claims.claim: TNF-α, FasL and other members of the TNF family contain S/TXXS/T sequences and proline-rich domains that can bind adaptor proteins and transduce signals.
claims.source: For example, TNF-α, FasL and other members of the TNF family, contain S/TXXS/T sequences and proline-rich domains (FasL) that can bind adaptor proteins and thereby transduce signals (Kennelly and Krebs, 1991; Watts et al., 1999; Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007; Amanchy et al., 2011; Daar, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kennelly and Krebs, 1991; Watts et al., 1999; Eissner et al., 2004; Sun and Fink, 2007; Amanchy et al., 2011; Daar, 2012).

claims.claim: Ephrins and semaphorins signal through PDZ-binding motifs and proline-rich domains.
claims.source: In contrast, ephrins and semaphorins signal through PDZ-binding motifs and also proline-rich domains (Klein, 2009; Zhou et al., 2008; Daar, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Klein, 2009; Zhou et al., 2008; Daar, 2012).

claims.claim: Potential activation sites in transmembrane chemokines include cytoplasmic SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites (YXPV/R).
claims.source: Potential activation sites include cytoplasmic SXXS-sequences (comparable to those of the TNF family) and additionally SH2-binding sites (YXPV/R).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and comparison with known signaling motifs, as shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: In CX3CL1, SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals.
claims.source: In CX3CL1, both sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals; in the case of CXCL16, they are found – as far as known - in primates and only same mammals (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: In CXCL16, SXXS-sequences and SH2-binding sites are found in primates and only some mammals.
claims.source: In CX3CL1, both sites are highly conserved from monotremes through marsupials to highly developed mammals; in the case of CXCL16, they are found – as far as known - in primates and only same mammals (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The expression of transmembrane chemokines can be induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α, IFN-γ and interleukin-1β in fibroblasts and endothelial cells.
claims.source: The expression of transmembrane chemokines can be induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α, IFN-γ and interleukin-1β, e.g. in fibroblasts and endothelial cells (Garcia et al., 2000; Abel et al., 2004; Isozaki et al., 2011) regulating their role in inflammatory (trans-) migration processes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Garcia et al., 2000; Abel et al., 2004; Isozaki et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The release of the chemokine domain is mediated by the cell surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 in a constitutive or cytokine-induced manner.
claims.source: The release of the chemokine domain is mediated by the cell surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 in a constitutive (mainly ADAM10) or cytokine-induced manner (Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Abel et al., 2004; Ludwig et al., 2005).

claims.claim: ADAM17 was initially discovered as TNF-α-converting enzyme (TACE) liberating soluble cytokine from the transmembrane form.
claims.source: ADAM17 was initially discovered as TNF-α-converting enzyme (TACE) liberating soluble cytokine from the transmembrane form.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ADAM17/TACE.

claims.claim: ADAMs are supposed to terminate reverse signaling by cleaving transmembrane ligands of the TNF family bound to their receptors.
claims.source: ADAMs are supposed to terminate reverse signaling by cleaving transmembrane ligands of the TNF family bound to their receptors (Sun and Fink, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun and Fink, 2007.

claims.claim: In the case of ephrin-A, ADAM10 is constitutively associated with the EphA receptor and cleaves ephrin-A5 in trans upon ligand binding.
claims.source: In case of ephrin-A, ADAM10 is constitutively associated with the EphA receptor that clusters and is activated upon ligand binding; this positions the proteinase domain for effective ephrin-A5 cleavage and the cleavage occurs in trans, with ADAM10 and its substrate being on the membranes of opposing cells (Janes et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Janes et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells.
claims.source: We suppose that inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells that in tumors supports stabilization and proliferation.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings regarding the biological role of inverse signaling.

claims.claim: In tumors, inverse signaling supports stabilization and proliferation.
claims.source: We suppose that inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system in the communication between cells that in tumors supports stabilization and proliferation.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation supported by the observed anti-apoptotic and proliferative effects in tumor cells shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claims.claim: Inverse signaling appears to induce mainly autocrine stimulatory and stabilizing effects like increased proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
claims.source: As far as we know, inverse signaling of transmembrane chemokines appears to induce mainly autocrine stimulatory and stabilizing effects like increased proliferation and anti-apoptosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing proliferation enhancement and anti-apoptotic effects in Figures 3 and 7.

claims.claim: Tumors would profit from the positive feedback provided by inverse signaling.
claims.source: Obviously, tumors would clearly profit from such positive feedback.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the observed pro-survival and proliferative effects of inverse signaling in tumor cells.

claims.claim: Autocrine loops are important in many types of tumors, as exemplified by growth factors like EGF or PDGF.
claims.source: The importance of autocrine loops in many types of tumors becomes obvious regarding for example growth factors like epidermal (EGF) or platelet-derived (PDGF) growth factors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about autocrine signaling in cancer biology.

claims.claim: Stabilizing autocrine loops may play important roles in inflammation or under non-pathological conditions in tissue development.
claims.source: However, also in inflammation or under non-pathological conditions in tissue development these stabilizing autocrine loops may play important roles.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculative extension of the findings to other biological contexts.

claims.claim: Inverse signaling is a novel mechanism where soluble ligands shed from transmembrane counterparts induce signals through binding to the transmembrane ligands.
claims.source: Inverse signaling is an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning systems in the communication between cells. Here, soluble ligands that are shed from their transmembrane counterparts induce signals through binding to the transmembrane ligands.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the novel mechanism described throughout the manuscript and is supported by the collective experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor.
claims.source: Whereas reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor, the inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
claims.evidence: This claim distinguishes inverse signaling from reverse signaling based on established knowledge about reverse signaling mechanisms.

claims.claim: Inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
claims.source: Whereas reverse signaling requires the binding of the transmembrane ligand to its classical membrane-bound or soluble receptor, the inverse signaling depends on binding of the soluble ligand to its transmembrane counterpart.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the binding experiments shown in Figure 5 and the functional studies throughout the manuscript.

results.result: Transmembrane chemokines CXCL16 and CX3CL1 are widely expressed in various tumor cell lines (glioma, neuroblastoma, colon carcinoma) and endothelial cells, while their classical receptors CXCR6 and CX3CR1 are restricted to activated T-cells and monocytes but absent in tumor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C19-C28 are well-supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1) and immunocytochemistry showing high tm-chemokine expression in multiple tumor types with absent or minimal receptor expression. The expression pattern is consistently demonstrated across multiple cell lines with appropriate controls (LOX cells as negative control).

results.result: Receptor-negative but tm-chemokine-expressing cells (glioma cell lines and primary cultures) respond to soluble chemokines with transient, dose- and time-dependent ERK phosphorylation (10-40 min, maximum at ~1 nM), while tm-chemokine-negative LOX cells show no response.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C29-C33 are strongly supported by Western blot data (Figures 2A-C) and immunocytochemistry (Figure 2B) demonstrating ERK phosphorylation in multiple cell lines and primary cultures. The dose-response and time-course experiments are well-controlled with appropriate positive controls (EGF) and negative controls (LOX cells).

results.result: Soluble chemokines bind with high affinity to cells expressing transmembrane chemokines, as demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy, FACS, electron microscopy, and chemical cross-linking showing association of 1-2 soluble peptides to tm-chemokines.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C48-C53 are supported by multiple complementary binding assays (Figure 5A-D) including fluorescence microscopy, FACS analysis, immuno-electron microscopy, and cross-linking experiments. The use of multiple independent techniques strengthens the conclusion, though the stoichiometry inference (C53) is based on molecular weight estimation which has inherent uncertainty.

results.result: Soluble chemokines induce biological effects in tm-chemokine-expressing cells including ERK phosphorylation, enhanced proliferation (U343, A764 cells), and anti-apoptotic effects (reduced caspase-3/7 activity and PARP cleavage), while tm-chemokine-negative LOX cells do not respond.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C34-C36 are supported by Western blots (Figures 2, 6, 8), WST-assays (Figure 3), and caspase-3/7 activity assays (Figure 3). The biological effects are consistently observed across multiple cell lines with appropriate controls. Statistical significance is indicated for proliferation and anti-apoptosis assays.

results.result: Soluble chemokines do not mediate cell migration in glioma cells despite inducing other biological effects.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by wound healing assay data (Figure 3 bottom panel) showing no significant difference in migration compared to controls. This negative result is important for characterizing the specificity of inverse signaling and distinguishing it from classical chemokine receptor signaling.

results.result: The intracellular domain of transmembrane chemokines is required for inverse signaling, as C-terminally truncated tm-chemokines lacking this domain cannot transduce signals upon stimulation with soluble chemokines.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C55 are supported by experiments with truncated tm-chemokines (Figure 6B) showing abolished ERK phosphorylation. The truncation was verified by immunocytochemistry and Western blot. This structure-function analysis provides strong evidence for the requirement of the intracellular domain.

results.result: Dimerization of transmembrane chemokines is required for inverse signaling, as intact antibodies but not monovalent F(ab) fragments can induce ERK phosphorylation in tm-chemokine-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C63-C65 are supported by experiments comparing intact antibodies to F(ab) fragments (Figure 9). The differential response provides strong evidence for dimerization requirement. However, the claim is partially inferential as direct visualization of dimerization was not performed in this study, though it is supported by cited literature (C66, C67).

results.result: Transfection of tm-chemokine-negative LOX cells with full-length tm-chemokines confers responsiveness to soluble chemokines (ERK phosphorylation) and to conditioned media containing shed chemokines, and provides protection from Camptothecin-induced apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C56-C60 are supported by transfection experiments (Figures 6A, 6C, 7) showing gain-of-function in LOX cells. Transfection efficiency was verified by qRT-PCR and immunocytochemistry. The use of conditioned media (C56-C57) demonstrates that naturally shed chemokines can also induce signaling, strengthening the physiological relevance.

results.result: siRNA silencing of tm-chemokines in responsive glioma cells reduces tm-chemokine transcript levels to 24-59% of controls and clearly reduces s-chemokine-mediated ERK phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 are supported by siRNA experiments (Figure 8) showing loss-of-function. Silencing efficiency was confirmed by qRT-PCR, and reduced ERK phosphorylation was demonstrated by Western blot. This complementary approach to the gain-of-function experiments strengthens the conclusion that tm-chemokines mediate the observed signaling.

results.result: Inverse signaling is independent of classical G-protein coupled receptor signaling (Pertussis toxin insensitive), and alternative receptors including CXCR7, chemokine decoy receptors, US28, and CD44 can be excluded as mediators.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C47 are supported by Pertussis toxin experiments (Figure 4A), CXCR7 inhibition (Figure 4C), and expression profiling (Figure 4B). The systematic exclusion of alternative receptors strengthens the conclusion that tm-chemokines themselves mediate the signaling. However, the possibility of an unidentified co-receptor cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: CXCL16 and CX3CL1 are transmembrane proteins converted to soluble ligands by ADAM10/17, with potential signaling motifs in their intracellular domains, though signaling via transmembrane forms had not been previously described.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 are supported by citations to established literature and sequence analysis (Table 1). These claims establish the background knowledge and novelty of the current findings. The claims are appropriately attributed to prior work.

results.result: Reverse signaling by transmembrane ligands has been described for TNF family members, IL-15, ephrin-ligands, and semaphorins, inducing various biological functions including co-stimulation, silencing, and synapse formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 are supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims provide important context for understanding the novelty of inverse signaling and its relationship to reverse signaling. The claims are accurately attributed to prior work.

results.result: The intracellular domains of transmembrane chemokines contain potential signaling motifs (SXXS sequences and SH2-binding sites) similar to those in TNF family members and ephrins, with conservation patterns varying between CX3CL1 (highly conserved across mammals) and CXCL16 (primates and some mammals).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are supported by sequence analysis (Table 1) and comparison with known signaling motifs from literature. The evolutionary conservation analysis adds support for functional significance. However, the actual involvement of these specific motifs in inverse signaling requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Expression of transmembrane chemokines is induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines, and their shedding is mediated by ADAM10/17. ADAMs may terminate reverse signaling by cleaving transmembrane ligands, as demonstrated for TNF family and ephrin-A.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 are supported by citations to established literature. These claims provide important context for understanding the regulation of tm-chemokine expression and the potential role of ADAMs in modulating inverse signaling. The claims are appropriately attributed to prior work.

results.result: Dimerization and clustering of CX3CL1 chemokine domain and transmembrane CX3CL1 have been demonstrated by X-ray crystallography and BRET/HTRF studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by appropriate citations to prior structural and biophysical studies. These claims provide important supporting evidence for the dimerization requirement inferred from the antibody experiments in the current study.

results.result: Inverse signaling is proposed to be an autocrine feedback and fine-tuning system that supports tumor cell stabilization and proliferation, with potential roles in inflammation and tissue development.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 are largely speculative interpretations of the experimental findings. While the observed pro-survival and proliferative effects (C81) are supported by data, the broader biological significance and roles in different contexts (C79, C80, C82, C84) require further investigation. The comparison to autocrine growth factor loops (C83) is based on established knowledge but the specific role of inverse signaling in tumors needs validation in more physiological models.

results.result: Inverse signaling is a novel mechanism where soluble ligands shed from transmembrane counterparts induce signals through binding to transmembrane ligands, distinct from reverse signaling which requires binding of transmembrane ligand to its classical receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 summarize the key conceptual advance of the manuscript. The distinction between inverse and reverse signaling is clearly defined and supported by the collective experimental evidence including binding studies, signaling assays, gain- and loss-of-function experiments, and exclusion of classical receptors. This represents a novel signaling mechanism.
